$description: Every foreground/background combination Mizan intends to render, with the WCAG context each is used in. machinery/scripts/check-contrast.mjs resolves both tokens in every mode combination and fails the build when a declared pair falls below its threshold. An undeclared pairing is an unchecked pairing: nothing here means nothing verified, so coverage matters as much as strictness. The escape hatch is an explicit exception with a stated reason, never a lowered threshold — and an exception is reported in the build output whether it passes or fails, because a silent exception defeats the point of having a list. The context "decorative" is not an escape hatch but the absence of a claim: it says WCAG sets no bar for this pairing, so the ratio is reported and nothing is gated. It is legitimate only where 1.4.11 genuinely does not apply, and every use has to argue that in its own $description. See decisions/010-contrast-is-a-token-layer-guarantee.md.

pairs.$description: Body and heading text on the default surface. The most-used pairing in both products.
Body text inside a tinted panel. Sunken is lighter than the AA floor allows to be assumed, so it is checked separately from surface.default.
The second and last neutral text tier (decision 009). It resolves to a different value per product mode, so this pair is the one that proves the mode matrix rather than the base values.
Secondary text inside a tinted panel — the tightest neutral-on-neutral pairing in the system, and the first to break if either value drifts.

Label text on the primary action. action.primary resolves per product — green.600 in Market, blue.600 in Move (decision 008) — so this pair is two fills, not one, and both were set at the lightness that lets white sit on them: 5.64:1 on green.600 and 5.27:1 on blue.600. Theme never touches either, so the same two ratios hold in all four combinations. The blue is the binding case, and a brand change in either product has to clear 4.5 here before it ships.

The 1px neutral hairline around a card, and the divider between list rows. Declared decorative, which means the ratio is measured and reported but nothing gates it. WCAG 1.4.11 governs the boundaries that identify user interface components and their states; a container hairline identifies no component and carries no state, so it is not one. Declaring it "ui" would be a category error with a visible cost — it would force every card border to roughly #949494 or darker, which is a boxed-in, heavily ruled interface nobody asked for. Leaving it undeclared would be worse: an undeclared pairing is an unchecked one, and this is the most-drawn line in either product. So it is declared, resolved in every mode, and printed on every run — visible to the system, and not wrongly failed by it. The moment a border starts identifying a control, it is border.control, and that one is gated.
The boundary of an interactive control. Checked separately from border.default because a control edge carries more meaning than a divider and may not inherit the same value.
Discount pricing is read as text and priced as a promise, so it carries the full 4.5 text threshold rather than the indicator threshold.
Trip cancellation and other destructive mobility messaging. Text, so 4.5. Kept distinct from commerce.discount by decision 008 — value coincidence is not semantic identity.

INDICATOR ONLY. Amber cannot reach 4.5 without becoming brown, so this token is a dot, bar or badge fill and must never carry text (decision 008). Any text beside the indicator uses text.primary. Checked at the 3.0 non-text threshold precisely because the text use is forbidden — if this pair is ever declared as context text, the token is being misused.
INDICATOR ONLY, on the same terms as commerce.stock.low. Surge pricing is signalled by a graphic element; the price itself is text.primary. Never text (decision 008).
